name: Salience bias
statement: Whatever is conspicuous gets treated as the cause of what happened, or as the number worth acting on, while equally real but less visible features are discounted.
meaning: Two literatures use the word and they do not measure the same thing. In social psychology salience is perceptual prominence, meaning which person an observer happens to be looking at, and the claim is that the person in view is credited with driving the interaction. In economics salience is the weight a buyer puts on a cost that is real but not displayed, such as a sales tax added at the register. Chetty, Looney and Kroft turn this into a parameter they call theta, where a value of one means the tax is treated exactly like a price of the same size. Bordalo, Gennaioli and Shleifer go further and make salience a function of how far a payoff stands out from the other payoffs on offer, which makes it depend on what else is in the choice set. The social claim is about attributing causes. The economic claim is about how much a known cost counts. Evidence for one is not evidence for the other, and this entry keeps them apart.

origin.who: Shelley E. Taylor and Susan T. Fiske
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is 'Point of view and perceptions of causality', volume 32, pages 439 to 445. The word salience reaches the title of their work three years later, in the chapter 'Salience, Attention, and Attribution: Top of the Head Phenomena'. The economic literature that now carries the same word starts separately, with Chetty, Looney and Kroft in 2009 and Bordalo, Gennaioli and Shleifer in 2012. Neither cites the 1975 experiments. Chetty, Looney and Kroft cite no work by Taylor or Fiske at all, and the salience theory drafts take their definition of the word from Taylor and Thompson in 1982.

evidence: The strongest evidence is a field experiment on sales tax. Chetty, Looney and Kroft posted tax-inclusive price tags on about 750 cosmetics, hair care and deodorant products in one supermarket from 22 February to 15 March 2006. Weekly quantity sold per category fell by 2.20 units against untagged categories in the same store and against the same categories in two matched control stores, standard error 0.59, p below 0.01. Set against a base of 29 units a week, that is a fall of 7.6 percent. With a category price elasticity of 1.59 and a sales tax of 7.375 percent, the implied attention parameter is 0.35, so a ten percent tax rise moved demand as much as a 3.5 percent price rise. A classroom survey supplied the first stage: 18 percent of 49 students read the tax-inclusive total off the ordinary tags and 75 percent read it off the experimental ones. Finkelstein runs the argument backwards, from attention to policy. She assembled toll rates and electronic collection dates for 123 toll facilities in the United States. In her Massachusetts survey, 85 percent of drivers paying electronically misstated the toll they had just paid, against 31 percent of those paying cash. Once electronic collection reaches its steady state share of about 60 percent, she estimates tolls sit 20 to 40 percent above where they would otherwise have been. Bordalo, Gennaioli and Shleifer built the formal version, replacing true probabilities with weights tilted toward payoffs that stand out against the alternatives. It predicts something prospect theory does not: the Allais paradox should disappear when the two lotteries are shown paying their common consequence in the same state. Their 2010 working paper reports 79 percent of subjects on the diagonal, meaning they chose alike whether the common payoff was 0 or 2,400. Their revision of December 2011 prints a different table and reports 80 percent of choices on that diagonal. The published article could not be read for this entry, so neither figure can be called the published one. The attribution studies behind the other sense of the word are older, and a copy of the 1975 paper was read here. Taylor and Fiske seated 38 Harvard-Radcliffe students around two male confederates who held a standardised five-minute conversation. Observers facing confederate A rated him 20.25 on the combined causal-role measure against 15.54 for B. Observers facing B rated B 20.75 against 12.00, and observers sitting to the side split them 17.51 to 16.75. The viewpoint by confederate interaction gave F(2, 26) = 18.68, p < .001, and the authors report it accounting for more than 36 percent of the variance. A second experiment with 54 undergraduates watching videotape reproduced the effect where subjects were told which participant to watch, F(2, 12) = 5.55, p < .02. Where half the screen was covered instead, neither participant was seen as more causal.

examples.tag: The fare that is not the fare
examples.text: A traveller compares two flights on the headline price and books the cheaper, then pays again for a seat, a bag and the card fee. The extra charges were published and familiar, and they carried less weight in the choice because the headline number was the one on display.

examples.tag: The tax added at the till
examples.text: A shopper fills a basket against the shelf prices and treats the total at the register as a surprise, although the rate is posted and he could state it if asked. Knowing a cost is not the same as counting it, and the undisplayed part counts for less.

examples.tag: The person the camera was pointed at
examples.text: Watching a recording of a meeting, viewers describe whoever the camera faced as having driven the discussion. Which participant looked like the cause was settled by who was in shot, and the people out of shot had spoken no less.

replication.headline: Attention to sales tax came out at 0.25 in an online experiment with 2,998 shoppers, near the 0.35 measured in the supermarket, while the attribution effect's clearest repeat is the original authors' own follow-up.
replication.detail: Taubinsky and Rees-Jones ran an online shopping experiment through a market research panel. 4,328 consumers finished it and 2,998 survived the comprehension and coding rules, approximately matching the United States adult population on household income, gender and age. 982 of them faced the sales tax rates of their own city and 914 faced triple those rates. In the preferred specification average theta was 0.250 in the standard-tax arm, standard error 0.095, and 0.475 in the triple-tax arm, standard error 0.039, with the difference at p = 0.01. Using all the data the two figures are 0.261 and 0.481, difference p = 0.03. That brackets the 0.35 from the supermarket and adds a boundary condition, because attention is not a fixed trait and rises with the size of the tax. The published Review of Economic Studies article was obtained for this check, and its Table 2 carries the same numbers as the working paper. Salience theory has fared worse on the prediction that separates it from prospect theory. Loewenfeld and Zheng tested correlation sensitivity in the Allais common-consequence problem and in Mao pairs while controlling for event splitting, the tendency to weight an outcome more heavily when it is listed as two rows rather than one. Their abstract states that once event splitting is controlled, no consistent evidence for correlation effects remains. Only that abstract could be read, so none of their sample sizes or test statistics appear here. Bruhin, Manai and Santos-Pinto leave room for both accounts. Their finite mixture model assigned 37.9 percent of 283 subjects to the prospect theory type, 33.7 percent to the salience theory type and 28.4 percent to the expected utility type. Those subjects were mostly students of the University of Lausanne and the EPFL, recruited through ORSEE. For the attribution effect the repeats are older than the file drawer suggests. Taylor, Crocker, Fiske, Sprinzen and Winkler ran the follow-up themselves in 1979, three studies with 279 undergraduates watching the same kind of dyadic conversation. The abstract reports salience effects holding when the perceiver was distracted, whether impressions were taken at once or after a delay, when the conversation had high interest value, and when the perceiver joined the discussion. That article is paywalled, so its abstract is all that stands behind this paragraph. A preregistration to replicate Experiment 1 of the 1975 paper was posted on the Open Science Framework on 16 May 2017 by Nicholas Edwards and Alan Jern, under the Replication Recipe schema. Its archive holds the original paper, a confederate script and a videos folder, with no data and no results, and its parent project is not public. No publication reporting it was found in searches of Crossref, the Open Science Framework and the open web on 21 September 2026. The nearest repeat by other hands is the camera perspective bias, where Ware, Lassiter, Patterson and Ransom used eye tracking. Their abstract reports Experiment 1 reproducing the bias, with fixation duration partly mediating it.

study.cite: Taubinsky, D., & Rees-Jones, A. (2018). Attention variation and welfare: Theory and evidence from a tax salience experiment. The Review of Economic Studies, 85(4), 2462-2496.

limits: The supermarket result is one store, three weeks and three categories of toiletries, chosen because the chain would not risk its sales leaders and because impulse categories have high price elasticities. The authors state that they can estimate only the effect of posting the tags, and cannot separate raised tax salience from other consequences of hanging 750 new tags in one aisle. They lean on their beer analysis to cover that, and it is not a clean test either. A one percent rise in the gross-of-excise price cut beer consumption by 0.88 percent against 0.20 percent for the sales tax, but once state income and unemployment are controlled the sales tax coefficient falls to -0.01 while the excise coefficient moves to -0.91. Salience is also not the only mechanism that makes a hidden number bite. Bollinger, Leslie and Sorensen studied mandatory calorie posting at Starbucks in New York City, which began on 1 April 2008. The published abstract reports calories per transaction falling by 6 percent. The working paper puts the fall at 5.8 percent, worth 14.4 calories, with food calories down 13.7 percent and beverage calories down 0.3 percent, and the published article could not be obtained here. Their own test of mechanism cuts against salience: cardholders who bought both inside and outside New York changed their choices at non-posting stores too, which fits learning rather than salience. Revenue did not fall overall, and daily revenue rose 3.3 percent at the 37 New York stores sitting within 100 metres of a Dunkin Donuts.
misreadings: The two senses of the word get merged. A page that opens with Taylor and Fiske's seated observers and closes with a 7.6 percent drop in supermarket sales has fused a claim about who looks causal to a claim about how much a tax counts, and no study joins them. The tax figure is also quoted at its rounder end. The abstract says 8 percent; the paper's own calculation of 2.2 units against a base of 29 gives 7.6 percent. Neither number means shoppers were unaware of the tax. Chetty, Looney and Kroft surveyed 91 customers at the treatment store, and 82 percent correctly reported which items were taxable, with a mean estimate of the local rate of 7.48 percent against an actual 7.375 percent. People knew the tax and did not act on it, which is a different claim from ignorance, and it is the claim the parameter of 0.35 encodes. Calorie posting is often cited as salience failing. It did not fail. It moved calories per transaction by a margin close to the one the tax tags moved units sold, and what the authors question is the mechanism rather than the effect. The original attribution result is narrower than its retellings. Taylor and Fiske found that viewpoint moved who was seen as the causal agent, and their own abstract says the effect did not extend to seeing that person's behaviour as more dispositionally based. Last, salience theory in economics is a model of choice among gambles with a defined salience function, not a general statement that vivid things loom large. Its distinctive prediction concerns what happens when two lotteries are shown as correlated, and that prediction is the part currently in doubt. Its headline number also moves between drafts, from 79 percent of subjects in the 2010 working paper to 80 percent of choices in the revision of December 2011, so a page quoting it should say which draft it read.

Finkelstein, A. (2009). E-ZTax: Tax salience and tax rates. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 124(3), 969-1010. Figures here are read from the author's copy of the published article.

Bordalo, P., Gennaioli, N., & Shleifer, A. (2012). Salience theory of choice under risk. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 127(3), 1243-1285. The published article could not be fetched on 21 September 2026. The Oxford Academic PDF and the author's Harvard page both returned 403, and the Harvard DASH copy served a human-verification page instead of a file. Two earlier drafts were read instead, and this entry says which figure comes from which. The url here is National Bureau of Economic Research working paper 16387, the source for the 79 percent figure.

Bordalo, P., Gennaioli, N., & Shleifer, A. Salience theory of choice under risk. Revised manuscript dated December 2011, hosted by the Centre de Recerca en Economia Internacional. Source for the 80 percent figure and for the table of 7, 9, 11 and 73 percent, which differs from the 2010 working paper. It is a manuscript, not the published article.

Taubinsky, D., & Rees-Jones, A. (2018). Attention variation and welfare: Theory and evidence from a tax salience experiment. The Review of Economic Studies, 85(4), 2462-2496. Read in the published version, from an author's copy. Its Table 2 matches National Bureau of Economic Research working paper 22545 on every estimate quoted here.

Bollinger, B., Leslie, P., & Sorensen, A. (2011). Calorie posting in chain restaurants. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, 3(1), 91-128. The abstract was read at the American Economic Association listing, and it gives a fall of 6 percent. The full text is offered there as a free PDF, which returned 403 to two fetchers on 21 September 2026, so the itemised figures on this page come from National Bureau of Economic Research working paper 15648.

Loewenfeld, M., & Zheng, J. (2024). Salience or event-splitting? An experimental investigation of correlation sensitivity in risk-taking. Journal of the Economic Science Association, 10(2), 346-366. Read at the publisher's abstract page on Cambridge Core; the full text is paywalled. An open deposit exists at the French repository HAL, and on 21 September 2026 every route to it, including the file URL given by HAL's own search interface, returned a proof-of-work bot challenge rather than the file.

Bruhin, A., Manai, M., & Santos-Pinto, L. (2022). Risk and rationality: The relative importance of probability weighting and choice set dependence. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 65(2), 139-184. Read in the published full text, which is open at the publisher. The type shares quoted here are its own, to one decimal place.

A scan of the article is attached to the Open Science Framework registration listed below, and every figure quoted from the 1975 studies was read off that scan.
